lesson_title: Two Weak Things Make One Strong Thing
hook_text: Concrete snaps if you pull it. Wood splits if you push across it. So why are buildings made of both?
clip_script: Every material hates one force. Concrete is a rock you can pour: squash it and it laughs, pull it and it cracks at a tenth of the load. So engineers put steel exactly where the pull is. A beam on two walls stretches at the bottom, so the bars go near the bottom. Over a column it bends the other way, so the bars go near the top. The concrete squashes, the steel pulls, ribs make them grip, they expand together in heat, and the concrete keeps the steel from rusting. Wood hates being pulled across the grain and splits along it. So peel a log into thin sheets and glue an odd number crosswise. Now it is strong every way, a split stops at the next layer, and it stays flat. That is plywood, and that is a composite: each material where the force it is good at will act.
visual_style: Whiteboard beam on two walls bends; red tension zone at the bottom fills with steel bars; the beam flips over a column and the bars jump to the top; a log peels into sheets that stack with alternating grain arrows.
mood: Site-visit practical, clear, one big idea.
pacing: Concrete's weakness, bars at the bottom, bars at the top, plywood's crossed layers, the principle.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and look at the cut edge of any plywood sheet to count its layers.
